source_read: PDF, pp. 1-8 (all pages; no abstract is printed in this file; Fig. 2 (p. 4) and Fig. 3 (p. 5) read from the embedded 300-ppi images; pp. 1 and 3-7 checked on rendered pages at 150 dpi; every pooled estimate in Figs 2-3 recomputed from the printed counts)

claims.overstatement: No material overstatement: the claim keeps 'reported', 'met the criteria' and 'not a prevalence among people who currently use cocaine', and states the confounding and design limits. Two balance points: (1) it gives the review's cited statement that symptoms are usually transient and pass with abstinence (p. 1) but not the same paragraph's next statement that they can become more severe with continued use and last many weeks after last use; (2) it reports that other drug use could not be separated from cocaine but not the authors' counter-argument (p. 6) that alcohol and opioids are less likely to cause psychotic symptoms and that cannabis-induced psychosis is very unlikely to explain the findings (citing Tang 2007, no significant effect of concomitant use disorder after adjusting for age and sex). 'Volunteers' for the two laboratory studies is not the review's word (p. 3 says current-use studies included only outpatients).
claims.note: Part not supported: the population parenthesis places 'one psychiatric emergency unit' among the 17 lifetime studies (5286 people). In the source the psychiatric emergency series (Elangovan 1993, 12/30, CIPD) is one of the three current-use studies (p. 3, Results 3.2, 6th paragraph; Fig. 2, p. 4); the review describes the lifetime studies as recruited through outpatient addiction treatment except one inpatient study (Brady 1991). The claim then counts the same series again under current use. Also, 'mean age 37, 68% men' are means across all 20 studies (p. 3), not the 17. Two further points on setting the claim inherits from the review: one lifetime study (Reid 2004, 21/23) is a laboratory cocaine-challenge study (p. 3, Results 3.1), and two lifetime CIPD studies are titled in the reference list as therapeutic-community samples (Vergara-Moragues 2012; Gonzalez-Saiz 2014), so 'almost all outpatient' is the review's description, not something its own reference list bears out. Everything else checks: every number in the statement and magnitude is printed where expected, and every editors' calculation reproduces from the Fig. 3 counts with DerSimonian-Laird on the logit scale (variance 1/x + 1/(n-x), which reproduces the plot's study-level intervals): CIPD with its own tau2 (0.482) 16.0% (8.45 to 28.26); all 17 with their own tau2 (0.593) 55.6% (46.01 to 64.84), prediction interval (t, 15 df) 18.7 to 87.2; CIPS with its own tau2 (0.138) prediction interval (t, 11 df) 47.8 to 83.6; CIPS without Tang 2007 (or without Cubells 2005) 67.73% (62.05 to 72.92). The printed figures (68.42 [62.80; 73.55], 15.94 [10.65; 23.17], 55.63 [50.16; 60.97]) reproduce exactly when one common tau2 of 0.1597 (the residual between-study variance after the CIPS/CIPD split; residual Q 140.1, 15 df) is applied to both subgroups and to the overall estimate, which is why the printed overall interval is narrower; the Methods (p. 2) describe a standard random-effects model and do not mention this. The current-use figures also reproduce (50.23 [32.04; 68.36] with the plot's tau2 0.3248; 41.39 [29.51; 54.36] without Mooney). Lifetime n: CIPS 4711 + CIPD 575 = 5286; current 28 + 44 + 30 = 102. The SAPS-CIP figure at the top of the instrument range (84.2%) is the single study Vergara-Moragues 2014 (96/114 in Fig. 3), one of the two studies that counted one psychotic symptom as a case (p. 4, Results 3.4). The region figures (and the text's count of 13 US and 4 Spanish studies) reproduce only when the study labelled Roncero 2017 (422/767) is counted as North American (North America 11 studies 66.5%, residual I2 95%, as printed); the PDF does not give that study's country (Supplementary Table S1 not seen), and the text's label 'Europe (Spain and France)' has no French study in that group (Trape 2014, Martinique, falls in South America and the Caribbean).

anchors.extracted: PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO and PsycARTICLES searched to 31 August 2020 (English, human, adult limits). Included cross-sectional, case-control or cohort studies of people with current or past cocaine use that either excluded people with primary psychotic disorders (schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder) and mood disorders with psychotic features, or clearly separated them.

All 20 studies: 5388 participants; mean sample 269.2 (23 to 2192); mean 68% men (49 to 100%), two studies men only; mean age 37.0 years (23 to 45); mean age at first use 22.2 (11 studies, n = 1888); mean years of use 22.4 (7 studies, n = 916). Countries: USA 13, Spain 4, French Caribbean 1, Canada 1, Brazil 1. Age and sex are means across all 20 studies, not the 17 lifetime studies.

Other substance use reported by few studies. Lifetime-use studies: lifetime dependence on alcohol 56.5% (3 studies), opioids 30% (2), cannabis 32% (2). Current-use studies: current alcohol use 39.5% (2), opioids 50.1% (2), cannabis 39.7% (3), other stimulants 30.8% (1).

anchors.locator: Results 3.1, 1st paragraph; 3.2, 3rd, 5th and 6th paragraphs (6th continues on p. 4)
anchors.extracted: 3 current-use and 17 lifetime-use studies; all cross-sectional except three cocaine-challenge studies (Kalayasiri 2006b, Mooney 2006, Reid 2004). Samples were people seeking or in treatment; lifetime studies recruited through outpatient addiction treatment centres except one inpatient study (Brady 1991). Current-use studies: one series of consecutive referrals to a psychiatric emergency unit (Elangovan 1993) and two laboratory cocaine-challenge studies (Kalayasiri 2006b, Mooney 2006). Pavon 2013 excluded as overlapping with Araos 2015; Herbeck 2006 and Vorspan 2012 also excluded.

anchors.locator: Results 3.3, 2nd-4th paragraphs; 3.4, 1st paragraph; with p. 1, Introduction, right column, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: 13 studies assessed cocaine-induced psychotic symptoms (CIPS), mostly with the CEQ or SAPS-CIP, several with study-specific questions; five assessed DSM cocaine-induced psychotic disorder (CIPD) by semi-structured interview, PRISM in four (Araos 2015, Elangovan 1993, Gonzalez-Saiz 2014, Vergara-Moragues 2012) and MINI in one (Willi 2017). Two studies counted a single psychotic symptom as a case (Miguel 2018; Vergara-Moragues 2014), rated high risk of bias for case definition. The CEQ mainly measures cocaine-induced paranoia, with other features such as hallucinations (p. 1).

Current use, 3 studies, n = 102: pooled 50.2% (95% CI 32.0 to 68.4), I2 66%. Fig. 2: Kalayasiri 2006b 12/28 (42.9%) and Mooney 2006 29/44 (65.9%), both symptom definitions (laboratory challenge studies); Elangovan 1993 12/30 (40.0%), disorder definition (psychiatric emergency series). Without Mooney 41.4% (29.5 to 54.4), I2 0%. Symptom subgroup 55.2% (32.8 to 75.7), disorder subgroup 40.0% (14.9 to 71.7). Reproduced: 50.23% (32.04 to 68.36) with the plot's tau2 0.3248.

Lifetime use, 17 studies, n = 5286: pooled 55.6% (50.2 to 61.0), I2 97% (Q 501, 16 df). Symptom subgroup 13 studies 68.4% (62.8 to 73.5); disorder subgroup 4 studies 16% (10.6 to 23.2); I2 89% in each; residual I2 89%. Fig. 3 prints the same tau2 (0.1597) for both subgroups and the overall estimate. Editors' calculations reproduced: all 17 with their own tau2 55.6% (46.0 to 64.8), prediction interval 18.7 to 87.2; disorder subgroup with its own tau2 16.0% (8.5 to 28.3); symptom subgroup prediction interval 47.8 to 83.6.

By instrument (lifetime): CEQ 6 studies 70.1% (62.6 to 76.7), I2 50; SAPS-CIP 1 study 84.2% (69.0 to 92.7) (= Vergara-Moragues 2014, 96/114 in Fig. 3); study-specific questions 6 studies 63.4% (55.2 to 70.9), I2 94%; PRISM 3 studies 11.7% (7.4 to 17.9); MINI 1 study 35.8% (18.9 to 57.1). Residual I2 87.

By region (lifetime): North America 66.5% (57.6 to 74.3), South America and Caribbean 56.1% (34.2 to 75.5), Europe 25.1% (15.1 to 38.6); I2 91%, 78%, 98%; residual I2 95%. Reproduced (66.5, 56.1, 25.1; residual I2 95.0%) with Roncero 2017 counted in North America.

anchors.locator: Fig. 3, symptom-subgroup rows; reference list pp. 7-8
anchors.extracted: Cubells 2005 and Tang 2007 both print 181/243 (74.49%, weight 6.9% each); their reference entries share authors (Cubells, Tang, Farrer). Floyd 2006 (36/51) and Zaytas 2013 (1500/2192, the largest study) appear in Fig. 3 but are not named in the text and have no reference-list entry. Without Tang 2007 the symptom subgroup is 67.7% (62.1 to 72.9) with its own tau2 (editors' calculation reproduced).

anchors.locator: Discussion 4.2, 3rd paragraph (left column) and 1st paragraph of right column; Results 3.9, last paragraph (pp. 5-6)
anchors.extracted: Cocaine use went with other drug use in all studies, so the authors cannot be certain cocaine is directly responsible for the psychotic symptoms; the contribution of alcohol and opioids could not be determined (authors argue their propensity to cause psychotic symptoms is lower, and that cannabis-induced psychosis very unlikely explains the findings; Tang 2007 found no significant effect of concomitant use disorder after age and sex adjustment). No route-of-administration analysis was possible.

anchors.locator: Discussion 4.2, last paragraph; 4.3, 2nd-3rd paragraphs (3rd continues on p. 7); p. 7, 4.3, 4th-5th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Prevalence may be underestimated because of impaired insight into symptoms. Almost all studies cross-sectional with retrospective assessment of cocaine-use history, so causal conclusions are difficult. Dose and dependence severity, polysubstance use and route could not be explored; crack and powder could not be compared (p. 7). Samples mostly treatment seekers in outpatient clinics, emergency services or hospitals; prevalence could be inflated by selection and admission-rate (Berkson) bias (p. 7).

anchors.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph (left column) and right column, 1st paragraph; with p. 7, Discussion 4.4, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Citing Vorspan 2012 (itself excluded from the meta-analysis, p. 3): in most cases the symptoms are transient and usually disappear with abstinence, but they can become more severe with continued use and last many weeks after last use. Citing Murrie 2020: no study reported transition rates from cocaine-induced psychotic disorder to schizophrenia (mean transition 22% for amphetamine-induced psychotic disorder). p. 7: transition rate from CIP to schizophrenia not known. Neither was measured in this review.

key_findings.correction: Minor wording: the review calls the two current-use laboratory studies cocaine challenges under controlled laboratory conditions (pp. 3-4); 'self-administration' is the wording of the Kalayasiri 2006b title only.

Editors' calculations in the note reproduced from the Fig. 3 counts: all 17 with their own tau2 0.593, 55.6% (46.0 to 64.8), prediction interval 18.7 to 87.2; CIPD with its own tau2 0.482, 16.0% (8.5 to 28.3).

Fig. 2 labels the two laboratory studies as symptom (CIPS) studies; 'paranoia' comes from their reference titles. Reproduced: 50.23% (32.04 to 68.36) with the plot's tau2 0.3248; 41.39% (29.51 to 54.36) without Mooney.

The figures and the note's best fit are confirmed (dropping Vergara-Moragues 2014, Miguel 2018 and Willi 2017 gives 55.6% (50.5 to 60.6), CIPS 68.3% (63.2 to 73.1), CIPD 11.7% (7.7 to 17.4), I2 97%, residual 86%, CIPD I2 0%, all as printed). But 'left the estimates almost unchanged' holds only for the overall and CIPS estimates: the CIPD estimate fell from 16% (4 studies, I2 89%) to 11.7% (I2 0%) once the one MINI study (Willi 2017, 35.8%) was dropped. Suggested: 'left the overall (55.6%) and symptom (68.3%) estimates almost unchanged; the disorder estimate fell to 11.7% (3 PRISM studies, I2 0%)'.
Wording: the authors say causal conclusions are 'difficult' to draw (p. 6, 4.3, 2nd paragraph), not that the designs do not allow them.

reporting_issues.note: No abstract or keywords in this PDF (p. 1). The corrigendum was not looked for, as instructed.

Reproduced: with tau2 0.1597 every printed Fig. 3 weight (1.8% to 7.8%) and the overall 55.63% (50.16 to 60.97) match exactly; standard DerSimonian-Laird on the 17 studies gives tau2 0.593 and 46.0 to 64.8. Fig. 2 uses the CIPS tau2 (0.3248), which is what widens the single Elangovan 1993 subgroup interval to 14.9 to 71.7. Printed interval width 10.8 points against 18.8.
Reproduced: without Tang 2007, CIPS 67.73% (62.05 to 72.92), all 16 studies 54.24% (44.10 to 64.04), each with its own tau2.
Neither name occurs anywhere in the text or reference list; 2192 of 5286 = 41.5%.

Small addition: 'every other interval' is not quite right. South America and Caribbean 56.1% (34.2 to 75.5) is also slightly off-centre on the logit scale (centre of bounds 55.9%). Recomputation from the Fig. 3 counts with the region model's common tau2 gives 56.1% (34.2 to 75.9), so 75.5 may also be mistyped; inconsequential.
The two laboratory studies hold 72 of the 102 current-use participants.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low confidence stands on items 4, 7 and 15 alone, whatever item 11 is judged. Item 2 'partial yes' is generous: registration 24 days before submission, with the search run after submission, suggests registration while the review was under way.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: 'cocaine users' in the title against treatment samples; 'cocaine-induced' against the authors' own statement that cocaine cannot be shown to be directly responsible; and a current-use 'prevalence' built mainly from two laboratory studies.

missed: The SAPS-CIP figure at the top of the instrument range (84.2%) is a single study, Vergara-Moragues 2014 (96/114 in Fig. 3, p. 5). It is one of the two studies that counted one psychotic symptom as a case (p. 4, 3.4), and by the card's own best fit it is one of the three dropped from the low-risk analysis. The highest instrument figure therefore rests on the loosest case definition.

Setting: the review says lifetime studies recruited through outpatient addiction treatment except one inpatient study (p. 3). But two lifetime CIPD studies are titled in the reference list as therapeutic-community samples (Vergara-Moragues 2012; Gonzalez-Saiz 2014, pp. 7-8), and one lifetime study (Reid 2004, 21/23, men only) is a laboratory cocaine-challenge study (p. 3, 3.1). The card's 'mostly outpatient' follows the review's text.

Elangovan 1993 is said to have used the PRISM (p. 4, 3.3), but the review's own reference for that instrument is dated 1996 (Hasin et al., 1996, p. 7). The instrument attribution for a 1993 study is doubtful, and with it that study's 'disorder' label in Fig. 2.

The region subgroups (and the text's count of 13 US and 4 Spanish studies, p. 3) reproduce only when the study labelled Roncero 2017 (422/767) is counted as North American; Trape 2014 then sits in South America and the Caribbean. The PDF does not give that study's country, so this should be checked against Supplementary Table S1 before the region figures are cited.
